summary: Madison Taylor's October 12, 2023 article presents autumn national festivals as expressions of a nation's culture, history and "romance" with its homeland. It surveys several festivals held in September and October 2023 across US cities, each illustrated with a quote from an organizer or participant. Themes include tradition, freedom, rivers, historical reenactment, food, patriotism and passing cultural pride between generations.
one_line: Madison Taylor's 2023 article surveys autumn US national festivals as expressions of cultural identity, heritage, patriotism and love of homeland.
key_facts: The article "National Festivals: Windows to a Nation's Soul" was written by Madison Taylor and dated October 12, 2023.
The Harvest Moon Festival took place on September 5, 2023 in the streets of Savannah and featured a lantern release.
Jasmine Henderson, chairperson of the festival committee, said the Harvest Moon Festival's lantern release symbolizes "releasing our shared hopes to the heavens."
The Liberty Parade was held on September 15th in Philadelphia, with floats, music and patriotic display.
Thomas Carter, a veteran parader since youth, said marchers are "recommitting to the values that forged this great nation."
The River Songs Festival began September 20th, 2023 on the banks of the Mississippi; Lila Martinez sang atop a gilded barge.
Arnold Black, festival director of River Songs, called the festival "our love song, our ode to the rolling tides of history and progress."
Great Frontier Days ran September 25th through 27th in Cheyenne, with authentic encampments, powwows and reenacted skirmishes.
Eleanor Wilson, a history teacher and reenactor, described each Great Frontier Days performance as "a love affair with the resilience of the human spirit."
The Flavors of the Nation Fair was held in New Orleans on October 3rd, featuring dishes such as jambalayas and pralines.
Chef Remi Lafontaine called the Flavors of the Nation Fair "a palatable renaissance."
The Revolutionary Revels took place September 30th in colonial Williamsburg; choreographer Emily Davis said the dances are "intimate conversations with patriotism."
Historian Jacob Moreno spoke at the Appalachian Artisan Festival on October 10th about crafts bridging past and present.
